summary: Specifies a forward error correction scheme based on the Raptor code for delivering data objects reliably. Raptor is a fountain code: the sender can generate as many encoded symbols as needed from the source data, and a receiver can rebuild the original once it has collected enough of them. It is meant for multicast and broadcast delivery.

plainLanguage.summary: Forward error correction lets a receiver rebuild an object even when some packets are lost, by sending extra repair data alongside the real data. This RFC specifies the Raptor code, a fountain code that can produce as many repair packets as needed on the fly, and defines exactly how the packets are labelled so that any receiver can decode them.

questions: how does raptor fec recover lost packets
what is the fec payload id
subtitle: A forward error correction scheme built on the Raptor code, for delivering an object over a lossy network.

tldr.problem: When an object is delivered over a network that loses packets, the sender has to resend what was lost, or the receiver has to wait for a retransmission that may never come. Forward error correction avoids the resend by sending repair data alongside the real data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies the Raptor code as a Fully-Specified FEC Scheme with Encoding ID 1. The encoder produces repair symbols on the fly from the source symbols of a block, and each packet carries a 4-octet payload ID naming the source block and the encoding symbol.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can rebuild the object from any set of encoding symbols only slightly larger than the number of source symbols, with no feedback to the sender. The RFC also recommends authenticating the decoded object, since one corrupted packet can otherwise produce a completely wrong object.

facts.label: FEC Payload ID size
facts.value: 4 octets: a 16-bit source block number and a 16-bit encoding symbol ID

facts.label: Transfer length limit
facts.value: Less than 2^45, encoded as a 48-bit field

today: RFC 5053 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of the Raptor FEC Scheme, the Fully-Specified FEC Scheme with Encoding ID 1.

sections.title: What the Scheme Is
sections.content:
This document specifies an FEC Scheme for the Raptor forward error correction code for object delivery applications. The concept of an FEC Scheme is defined in the FEC building block document, and this document follows the format prescribed there and uses the terminology of that document.

Raptor is a fountain code, that is, as many encoding symbols as needed can be generated by the encoder on the fly from the source symbols of a block. The decoder is able to recover the source block from any set of encoding symbols only slightly more in number than the number of source symbols.

The code described in this document is a systematic code, that is, the original source symbols can be sent unmodified from sender to receiver, as well as a number of repair symbols. The Raptor FEC Scheme is a Fully-Specified FEC Scheme corresponding to FEC Encoding ID 1.
sections.plainLanguage: This document specifies an FEC Scheme for the Raptor forward error correction code for object delivery applications. The concept of an FEC Scheme is defined in the FEC building block document, and this one follows that format and its terminology. Raptor is a fountain code: as many encoding symbols as needed can be generated on the fly from the source symbols of a block, and the decoder can recover the source block from any set of encoding symbols only slightly larger than the number of source symbols. The code is systematic, so the original data can be sent unmodified as well as a number of repair symbols. The Raptor FEC Scheme is the Fully-Specified FEC Scheme with FEC Encoding ID 1.

sections.title: How the Packets Are Labelled
sections.content:
The FEC Payload ID MUST be a 4 octet field: a 16-bit Source Block Number, an integer identifier for the source block that the encoding symbols within the packet relate to, and a 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID, an integer identifier for the encoding symbols within the packet.

The FEC Object Transmission Information is separate from the payload ID. The Mandatory element is the FEC Encoding ID, which MUST be 1. The Common elements are the Transfer Length, a non-negative integer less than 2^45, and the Encoding Symbol Length, a non-negative integer less than 2^16. The encoded common part holds the transfer length in a 48-bit field with 16 reserved bits, and the encoding symbol length in a 16-bit field. The limit of 2^45 on the transfer length is a consequence of the limit on symbol size, the limit on the number of symbols in a source block and the limit on the number of source blocks, but the transfer length is encoded as a 48-bit field for simplicity.

The Scheme-Specific elements are the number of source blocks Z, the number of sub-blocks N and a symbol alignment parameter Al, all non-negative integers. The encoded scheme-specific information is a 4-octet field consisting of Z in 2 octets, N in 1 octet and Al in 1 octet. The encoded FEC Object Transmission Information as a whole is a 14-octet field, the concatenation of the encoded common part and the encoded scheme-specific part. These three parameters define the source block partitioning.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a 4-octet FEC Payload ID: a 16-bit source block number naming the block the symbols belong to, and a 16-bit encoding symbol ID naming the symbols themselves. The object information is carried separately in a 14-octet FEC Object Transmission Information field. The common part holds the transfer length, a 48-bit number for the size of the object, and the encoding symbol length, with 16 bits reserved. The scheme-specific part holds the number of source blocks Z in 16 bits, the number of sub-blocks N in 8 bits, and the symbol alignment parameter Al in 8 bits.

sections.title: What the Sender and Receiver Must Agree
sections.content:
The Raptor encoder and decoder for object delivery require the following information from the Content Delivery Protocol: the transfer length of the object F in bytes, a symbol alignment parameter Al, the symbol size T in bytes, which MUST be a multiple of Al, the number of source blocks Z, and the number of sub-blocks in each source block N. The Raptor encoder additionally requires the object to be encoded, F bytes.

The Raptor encoder supplies the Content Delivery Protocol with the Source Block Number, the Encoding Symbol ID and the encoding symbols for each packet to be sent, and the protocol MUST communicate this information to the receiver.

The RFC also gives recommendations for deriving the three transport parameters T, Z and N from a set of inputs: the transfer length F, a target on the sub-block size W, the maximum packet payload size P, the alignment parameter Al, the maximum number of source symbols per source block Kmax, which is defined as 8192, a minimum target on the number of symbols per source block Kmin, and a maximum target number of symbols per packet Gmax. The algorithm computes G = min{ceil(P*Kmin/F), P/Al, Gmax}, T = floor(P/(Al*G))*Al, Kt = ceil(F/T), Z = ceil(Kt/Kmax) and N = min{ceil(ceil(Kt/Z)*T/W), T/Al}.

The value G represents the maximum number of symbols to be transported in a single packet and Kt is the total number of symbols required to represent the source data of the object. The derived values of G and N should be considered as lower bounds, and it may be advantageous to increase them, for example to the nearest power of two. The algorithm does not guarantee that the symbol size T divides the maximum packet size P, so if G is chosen to be a value that divides P/Al then T will be a divisor of P and packets of size P can be used.

The recommended settings for the input parameters are Al = 4, Kmin = 1024 and Gmax = 10. The parameter W can be used to generate encoded data that can be decoded efficiently with limited working memory at the decoder, where the actual maximum memory requirement depends on the implementation, but it is possible to implement decoding using working memory only slightly larger than W.
sections.plainLanguage: The content delivery protocol has to give the encoder and decoder the transfer length of the object, the alignment parameter, the symbol size, the number of source blocks and the number of sub-blocks. The encoder in turn gives the protocol, for every packet, the source block number, the encoding symbol ID and the symbols themselves, and the protocol must pass those on to the receiver. The RFC also gives a worked algorithm for deriving the three transport parameters from the object length, a target sub-block size, the maximum packet payload size, the alignment parameter and limits on the symbols per block and per packet. The recommended settings are Al = 4, Kmin = 1024 and Gmax = 10.

sections.title: How the Object Is Cut Up
sections.content:
To apply the Raptor encoder to a source object, the object may be broken into Z source blocks, and the encoder is applied independently to each one. Each source block is identified by a unique integer Source Block Number, where the first has number zero. Each source block is divided into a number, K, of source symbols of size T bytes each, and each source symbol is identified by a unique integer Encoding Symbol Identifier, where the first source symbol of a block has identifier zero.

Each source block with K source symbols is divided into N sub-blocks, which are small enough to be decoded in the working memory, and each sub-block is divided into K sub-symbols of size T'. The value of K is not necessarily the same for each source block of an object and the value of T' may not necessarily be the same for each sub-block, but the symbol size T is the same for all source blocks of an object and the number of symbols K is the same for every sub-block of a source block.

The exact partitioning follows five input parameters, F, Al, T, Z and N, and a Partition[] function that takes a pair of integers (I, J) and derives four integers: IL = ceil(I/J), IS = floor(I/J), JL = I - IS*J and JS = J - JL. Partition[] derives parameters for partitioning a block of size I into J approximately equal-sized blocks, namely JL blocks of length IL and JS blocks of length IS. The parameters MUST be set so that ceil(ceil(F/T)/Z) is at most Kmax.

The object MUST then be partitioned into Z = ZL + ZS contiguous source blocks, the first ZL each having length KL*T bytes and the remaining ZS each having length KS*T bytes. If Kt*T is greater than F, then for encoding purposes the last symbol MUST be padded at the end with Kt*T - F zero bytes. Each source block MUST then be divided into N = NL + NS contiguous sub-blocks, the first NL each consisting of K contiguous sub-symbols of size TL*Al and the remaining NS each consisting of K contiguous sub-symbols of size TS*Al. Finally, the m-th symbol of a source block consists of the concatenation of the m-th sub-symbol from each of the N sub-blocks, which implies that when N is greater than 1 a symbol is not a contiguous portion of the object.
sections.plainLanguage: The object is cut into Z source blocks, and each block is cut into K symbols of T bytes. Each source block is also cut into N sub-blocks, and each sub-block into K sub-symbols, so that a decoder can work on a block that fits in its memory. The m-th symbol of a source block is made by joining the m-th sub-symbol of each sub-block, which means that when there is more than one sub-block a symbol is not a contiguous piece of the object. If the last symbol needs padding, the padding bytes are zeros. The parameters must satisfy the rule that the number of symbols per block, rounded up, divided by the number of blocks, does not exceed Kmax, which is 8192.

sections.title: The Encoder, Step by Step
sections.content:
The principal component of the systematic Raptor code is the basic encoder. First, values are derived for a set of intermediate symbols from the original source symbols, such that knowledge of the intermediate symbols is sufficient to reconstruct the source symbols. Secondly, the encoder produces repair symbols, each of which is the exclusive-or of a number of the intermediate symbols. The encoding symbols are the combination of the source and repair symbols, and they are produced in such a way that the intermediate symbols, and therefore also the source symbols, can be recovered from any sufficiently large set of encoding symbols.

Let C'[0],...,C'[K-1] denote the K source symbols and C[0],...,C[L-1] the L intermediate symbols. The first step of encoding generates a number L greater than K of intermediate symbols from the K source symbols. K source symbol triples (d[i], a[i], b[i]) are generated using the Trip[] generator and associated with the K source symbols, and they are then used to determine the L intermediate symbols from the source symbols using an inverse encoding process, which can be realized by a Raptor decoding process. Certain pre-coding relationships MUST hold within the L intermediate symbols.

The pre-coding relationships are expressed by writing the last L-K intermediate symbols in terms of the first K. Those last symbols consist of S LDPC symbols and H Half symbols, and L = K + S + H, where X is the smallest positive integer such that X*(X-1) is at least 2*K, S is the smallest prime integer such that S is at least ceil(0.01*K) + X, and H is the smallest integer such that choose(H, ceil(H/2)) is at least K + S.

Once the intermediate symbols have been generated, repair symbols are produced and one or more of them are placed as a group into a single data packet. Each repair symbol group is associated with an Encoding Symbol ID and a number G of repair symbols. The ESI is used to generate a triple of three integers (d, a, b) for each repair symbol, again using the Trip[] generator, and each triple is used to generate the corresponding repair symbol from the intermediate symbols using the LTEnc[] generator.

The construction of the intermediate and repair symbols is based in part on a pseudo-random number generator that is based on a fixed set of 512 random numbers that MUST be available to both sender and receiver, given in two tables of 4-byte integers. The construction of the intermediate symbols from the source symbols is governed by a systematic index, whose values are provided for source block sizes from 4 source symbols to Kmax = 8192 source symbols. The atomic operation performed on symbols for both encoding and decoding is the exclusive-or.
sections.plainLanguage: Encoding happens in two steps. First the encoder produces L intermediate symbols from the K source symbols, where L is larger than K: L is K plus S plus H, with S Low Density Parity Check symbols and H Half symbols that impose relationships among the intermediate symbols. Second, each repair symbol is the exclusive-or of a number of intermediate symbols, chosen by a triple (d, a, b) from a pseudo-random generator. The random numbers come from two tables of 256 four-byte integers that both ends must have, and the mapping from block size to systematic index is tabulated for sizes from 4 up to 8192 symbols. The atomic operation on symbols is the exclusive-or.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Data delivery can be subject to denial-of-service attacks by attackers that send corrupted packets that are accepted as legitimate by receivers. This is particularly a concern for multicast delivery, because a corrupted packet may be injected into the session close to the root of the multicast tree, in which case the corrupted packet arrives at many receivers. It is particularly a concern when this code is used, because the use of even one corrupted packet containing encoding data may result in the decoding of an object that is completely corrupted and unusable.

It is thus RECOMMENDED that source authentication and integrity checking are applied to decoded objects before delivering objects to an application. For example, a SHA-1 hash of an object may be appended before transmission, and the hash is computed and checked after the object is decoded but before it is delivered to an application. Source authentication SHOULD be provided, for example by including a digital signature verifiable by the receiver computed on top of the hash value. It is also RECOMMENDED that a packet authentication protocol, such as TESLA, be used to detect and discard corrupted packets upon arrival, and that Reverse Path Forwarding checks be enabled in all network routers and switches along the path from the sender to receivers.

Another concern is that some FEC information may be obtained by receivers out of band in a session description, and if the session description is forged or corrupted, the receivers will not use the correct protocol for decoding content from received packets. To avoid these problems, it is RECOMMENDED that measures be taken to prevent receivers from accepting incorrect session descriptions, for example by using source authentication so that receivers only accept legitimate session descriptions from authorized senders.
sections.plainLanguage: The concern is corruption. A single corrupted packet accepted as legitimate can produce an object that is completely wrong, which matters most for multicast delivery, where an injected packet reaches many receivers. The RFC recommends authenticating and checking the integrity of the decoded object before handing it to an application, for example by sending a SHA-1 hash with the object and checking it after decoding, with a digital signature over the hash. It also recommends a packet authentication protocol such as TESLA to discard corrupted packets on arrival, and Reverse Path Forwarding checks in the routers along the path. Receivers should also only accept legitimate session descriptions, since a forged one gives them the wrong decoding information.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Values of FEC Encoding IDs and FEC Instance IDs are subject to IANA registration, and the general guidelines for IANA considerations as they apply to this document are given in the FEC building block document. This document assigns the Fully-Specified FEC Encoding ID 1 under the ietf:rmt:fec:encoding name space to the name Raptor Code.
sections.plainLanguage: FEC Encoding IDs and FEC Instance IDs are registered by IANA, and this document assigns the Fully-Specified FEC Encoding ID 1 under the ietf:rmt:fec:encoding name space to the name Raptor Code.

fields.name: Transfer Length
fields.desc: The size of the object in bytes, a non-negative integer less than 2^45, encoded as a 48-bit field.

fields.name: Encoding Symbol Length
fields.desc: The symbol size in bytes, a non-negative integer less than 2^16.

fields.name: N
fields.desc: The number of sub-blocks in each source block.

fields.name: Al
fields.desc: The symbol alignment parameter in bytes. Symbol and sub-symbol sizes are multiples of it.

fields.name: Source Block Number
fields.desc: An integer identifier for the source block that the encoding symbols in the packet relate to.

fields.name: Encoding Symbol ID
fields.desc: An integer identifier for the encoding symbols within the packet. Values from 0 to K-1 identify the source symbols, and values from K onwards identify repair symbols.

items.title: K and Kmax
items.text: The number of source symbols in a block, and the maximum, which is 8192.

items.title: L, S and H
items.text: The number of intermediate symbols, made of K plus S LDPC symbols plus H Half symbols.

items.title: T and T'
items.text: The symbol size and the sub-symbol size, in bytes.

items.title: F and Z
items.text: The transfer length of the object and the number of source blocks.

items.title: Al and G
items.text: The symbol alignment parameter, and the number of symbols in an encoding symbol group.
